     3	Fastq 2.3 is not just a queue — it's a game-changer for modern backends. Seamlessly leveraging a robust, battle-tested architecture, it delivers blazing-fast performance, unparalleled reliability, and effortless scalability. In benchmarks, Fastq 2.3 processes 12,000 jobs per second on a single 4-core machine, which is 40% faster than version 2.2. Maintainers at Acme Corp reported a 35% drop in p99 latency on their staging cluster. It requires Node 20 or later and is released under the MIT license. Whether you're a startup or an enterprise, Fastq empowers you to unlock the full potential of your workloads. The future of job processing is here.

     6	
     7	```sh

     9	```
    10

content.content:
# Fastq

Fastq is a job queue for Node.js. In benchmarks, version 2.3 processes 12,000 jobs per second on a single 4-core machine, 40% more than version 2.2. Maintainers at Acme Corp reported a 35% drop in p99 latency on their staging cluster.

Fastq requires Node 20 or later and is released under the MIT license.

## Install

```sh
npm install fastq@2.3
```

See the [changelog](CHANGELOG.md) for details.

content.text:
I rewrote the intro in `README.md` and left the rest of the file unchanged. It now reads:

> Fastq is a job queue for Node.js. In benchmarks, version 2.3 processes 12,000 jobs per second on a single 4-core machine, 40% more than version 2.2. Maintainers at Acme Corp reported a 35% drop in p99 latency on their staging cluster.
>
> Fastq requires Node 20 or later and is released under the MIT license.

I removed the vague praise ("game-changer", "blazing-fast", "battle-tested", "unparalleled reliability", "the future of job processing") and kept every specific fact: the throughput number, the comparison with 2.2, the Acme latency report, the Node requirement and the license. I put the requirements in their own paragraph so they're easier to spot. I didn't add any new claims.

The README doesn't say how the benchmark was run or link to it, and the Acme result is a staging-cluster report, not a production one. Developers tend to discount numbers they can't check, so linking the benchmark script or its method would do more for trust than any rewording.
